reason: The sources provide over 10 cross-validated claims across multiple independent sites detailing Huge-LQG's discovery, size, and cosmological implications.
story: In January 2013, astronomers led by Roger Clowes announced the discovery of a cosmic giant: the Huge Large Quasar Group, or Huge-LQG. Using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, the team mapped a cluster of 73 quasars—intensely luminous active galactic nuclei powered by supermassive black holes—located at a redshift of 1.27. Spanning an astonishing four billion light-years across, Huge-LQG was identified as the largest known structure in the observable universe at the time. Travelling across it at the speed of light would take four billion years. This colossal scale directly challenged the Cosmological Principle, which posits that matter should be uniformly distributed on scales larger than roughly one billion light-years. However, the reality of Huge-LQG remains actively disputed, with critics arguing the grouping may be a statistical fluke rather than a genuine physical structure.
angle: A structure of 73 quasars spanning four billion light-years was found to be so vast that light would take four billion years to cross it, directly challenging the assumption that the universe is smooth on large scales.

claims.claim: On January 11, 2013, astronomers announced the discovery of the Huge Large Quasar Group (Huge-LQG).
The discovery of Huge-LQG was led by Dr. Roger G. Clowes of the University of Central Lancashire.
Huge-LQG spans approximately four billion light-years across at its widest point.
Huge-LQG has a maximum principal dimension of about 1,240 megaparsecs.
Quasars are extremely luminous active galactic nuclei powered by supermassive black holes.
At the time of its discovery announcement, Huge-LQG was identified as the largest known structure in the observable universe.
Huge-LQG was identified using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey.
Huge-LQG has a mean redshift of z = 1.27.
The Cosmological Principle assumes that at sufficiently large scales, the universe is homogeneous.
Traveling at the speed of light, it would take four billion years to cross Huge-LQG.
Huge-LQG is located about 615 megaparsecs away from the Clowes & Campusano Large Quasar Group.
The physical reality of Huge-LQG as a bound structure is disputed by other scientists who consider it a potential statistical fluke.

disputed: Quasar count discrepancy: S1, S3, S4, S5, and S7 state Huge-LQG contains 73 quasars, whereas S2 states 74 quasars. The script should use 73 quasars as supported by the primary research paper sources.

Structure reality: Clowes et al. identified Huge-LQG as a genuine structure, but critical studies (such as Nadathur) argue it is a false positive result from parameter choices. Attribute in script as 'a proposed structure whose reality remains debated by scientists'.
